title: 3D-printed social place preference assays for aquatic larvae
author: Keira Nakamura
materials: Use a 3D printing software to design the model. In this example, Rhino is used. Open Rhino and select the desired units for the model. Rhino Rhino 8 Robert McNeel & Associates

steps.title: Determine arena dimensions and notches
steps.instruction: Sketch the arena to fit the focal larvae, record coordinate points, and set four notches in the walls that are the same depth as the acrylic sheet (typically 1.5875 mm). Ensure wall and base depth match the acrylic thickness.

steps.title: Create arena walls with ExtrudeCrv
steps.instruction: In Rhino, use the Polyline tool to draw the outer box outline, then apply ExtrudeCrv to raise the walls to the height determined above (do not include the base height).

steps.title: Thicken walls for 3D printing
steps.instruction: Select the walls, run OffsetSrf, press “Flip All” so arrows point inward, and enter the wall thickness as the Distance value to make the walls thick enough for printing and stability.

steps.title: Add a base to the arena
steps.instruction: Select the original polyline, run PlanarSrf, then ExtrudeSrf with a negative value equal to the wall depth so the base does not overlap the walls, producing a fully enclosed box.

steps.title: Create barrier boxes for notches
steps.instruction: Model a barrier box whose width covers the open space plus the distance needed to embed it halfway into the wall, set its depth equal to the acrylic thickness (1.5875 mm) and its height taller than the arena; repeat for the opposite arm.

steps.title: Subtract barrier boxes to form notches
steps.instruction: Use BooleanDifference to subtract the barrier boxes from the arena walls, creating the four notches.

steps.title: Finalize geometry and export STL
steps.instruction: Run OffsetSrf on walls and base to the preferred depth, convert all shapes to surfaces with PlanarSrf, merge them using BooleanMerge (or BooleanSplit if overlaps occur), then run MergeAllFaces for a single cohesive surface. Double‑check dimensions and save the file as .stl.

steps.title: 3D‑print the arena
steps.instruction: Print the .stl file on a 3D printer (e.g., Bambu Lab X1E).

steps.title: Design laser‑cut barrier inserts
steps.instruction: Create a polyline in Rhino for barrier walls that fit inside the notches, set the print width to Hairline for laser cutting, and optionally design solid or perforated walls (clear, black, or white acrylic) to manipulate visual or olfactory cues.

steps.title: Assemble arena and seal if needed
steps.instruction: Insert the laser‑cut barrier pieces into the notches; optionally glue inserts with rubber cement for a water‑tight seal (rubber cement can be removed later).

steps.title: Optional freehand arena design
steps.instruction: Draw a fully enclosed shape as a base image in Rhino, convert it to a surface with merging and smoothing functions, add height to create walls, then follow steps 5–7 to add notches before printing.

steps.title: Set up social place preference assay
steps.instruction: Place the focal tadpole in the arena centre, allow a 30‑minute acclimation period (00:30:00), then add stimuli (other tadpoles, objects, or odors) to the boxed‑off areas on either side of the arena.

steps.title: Record behavior from above
steps.instruction: Position a camera overhead to record the assay; multiple arenas can be run simultaneously if space and cameras permit.

steps.title: Run interaction period
steps.instruction: Allow the focal animal to interact with the stimuli for a set duration (01:00:00 in the described experiments).

steps.title: Analyze video data
steps.instruction: Process the recordings with analysis software (e.g., DeepLabCut 3.0 or BORIS 9.9). Use scripts to quantify time spent in each arena region, region‑switch frequency, and animal velocity.
